html:
In 2010 scientists announced that DNA from a tiny finger bone found in Denisova Cave, in the Altai Mountains of Siberia, belonged to a kind of archaic human never known before. They named them the Denisovans.

The bone had been dug up in 2008. A team at the Max Planck Institute in Leipzig, led by Svante Pääbo, read first its mitochondrial DNA, then its whole genome. It was the first time a human group was discovered from DNA rather than from the shape of bones. The Denisovans were close relatives of the Neanderthals and lived across Asia for hundreds of thousands of years.

They also mixed with modern humans. Papuans and other peoples of Melanesia carry a few percent Denisovan DNA. A Denisovan gene variant helps Tibetans live at high altitude. Since then a jaw from the Tibetan Plateau and a few other fossils have been linked to them. Pääbo won the Nobel Prize in 2022 for this work.
sum: In 2010 scientists announced that DNA from a tiny finger bone found in Denisova Cave, in the Altai Mountains of Siberia, belonged to a kind of archaic human never known before. They named them the Denisovans.
